title: Joshua Commissioned and the Law Handed Over
summary: Moses, now a hundred and twenty, tells Israel that the LORD himself will go ahead of them and that Joshua will lead them across the Jordan. He charges Joshua publicly to be strong and courageous, writes down the law, gives it to the priests and elders, and orders that it be read to all Israel every seventh year. At the Tent of Meeting God commissions Joshua, warns Moses that Israel will turn to other gods after his death, and tells him to write a song that will testify against them.
story: Moses' speeches are finished, and the book turns to succession. Israel has been told since Numbers 27 that Moses would not enter the land and that Joshua would lead in his place (see also Deuteronomy 1:37-38 and 3:28). This chapter makes the handover formal and public. It also makes sure the law will outlive Moses by putting it in writing, placing it in the care of the priests, and scheduling its public reading. Yet the chapter is shadowed by God's frank prediction that the people will break the covenant. That prediction sets up the Song of Moses in chapter 32, and it hangs over the whole history that follows in Joshua, Judges, Samuel, and Kings.
historical:
The scene is set on the plains of Moab at the end of the wilderness years, just before the crossing into Canaan. The date of these events depends on the date of the exodus, placed by some in the fifteenth century BC and by many others in the thirteenth. The kings Sihon and Og (verse 4), rulers of Amorite kingdoms east of the Jordan in Heshbon and Bashan, had been defeated in Numbers 21, and their land had been given to Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh.

The chapter's concern with writing, deposit, and public reading also has a later history. When a book of the law was found in the temple during King Josiah's repairs in about 622 BC, it was read aloud to the people and led to a covenant renewal (2 Kings 22-23). Many scholars identify that book with some form of Deuteronomy. After the return from exile, Ezra read the law to the assembled people during the Feast of Tabernacles (Nehemiah 8), a direct echo of the reading commanded in verses 10 to 13.
cultural:
Ancient Near Eastern treaties between great kings and their vassals often included instructions to deposit the written treaty in a temple, before the gods, and to read it aloud to the vassal's people at set intervals. Deuteronomy follows a similar pattern: the written law is placed beside the ark of the covenant, the gold-covered chest that held the stone tablets of the Ten Commandments and stood in the tabernacle's inner room (verses 24-26), and it is to be read every seven years. The resemblance helped Israel understand its relationship with God as a binding covenant with a king.

The reading was to happen in the year of remission, the seventh year when debts were released (15:1-11), during the Feast of Tabernacles, the autumn harvest festival when Israelites lived in temporary shelters to remember the wilderness. It was a pilgrimage feast, so the whole nation would be gathered at the central sanctuary. The audience is notably broad: men, women, children, and the foreigners living among Israel (verse 12). In a world where few could read, public reading was how a law became common knowledge. Songs served a similar purpose. A song memorized by children would survive long after scrolls were lost or ignored, which is why God tells Moses to teach Israel a song that will not be forgotten from the lips of their descendants (verse 21).
literary: The chapter alternates between public scenes and private revelation. Moses speaks to all Israel (verses 1-6), then to Joshua before all Israel (verses 7-8), then hands the law to the priests and elders (verses 9-13). The LORD then speaks privately at the Tent of Meeting (verses 14-23), and the chapter returns to Moses and the Levites (verses 24-30). The refrain “Be strong and courageous” appears three times (verses 6, 7, 23), first to the people, then to Joshua from Moses, then to Joshua from God, and it will carry over into Joshua 1. Two written witnesses bracket the chapter's second half: the song (verses 19-22) and the Book of the Law (verses 24-26). Both are to testify against Israel when it turns away. The chapter ends as a lead-in: Moses recites the words of the song, which follows in chapter 32.

outline.t: Moses' age and assurance: the LORD will go ahead of you
Moses charges Joshua before all Israel
The law written and read every seventh year
At the tent: Joshua summoned and Israel's apostasy foretold
The Book of the Law placed beside the ark

doctrines.note: The LORD himself goes ahead of Israel and promises never to leave or forsake them. Leadership changes, but God's presence does not; Joshua's courage rests on that fact rather than on his own gifts.

God's word is written down, kept safe, and read publicly to everyone, including children and foreigners. Scripture's authority does not depend on the living presence of the one who first delivered it.
God predicts Israel's unfaithfulness before they enter the land, saying he knows their inclination (verse 21). The chapter is realistic about the human heart, even among a redeemed people.

When Israel turns away, God will hide his face (verses 17-18). The worst judgment described is not a catastrophe as such but the withdrawal of God's presence, which the people themselves will recognize.

words.note: Chazaq, to be strong or firm, paired with amats, to be bold or courageous. The pair forms the refrain of this chapter and of Joshua 1. The strength in view is not bravado; it is steadiness grounded in the promise that God goes with you.

Azav, to leave or forsake. God promises that he will never forsake his people (verses 6, 8), yet he warns that they will forsake him (verse 16). The same verb names both God's faithfulness and Israel's coming unfaithfulness, a sharp and deliberate contrast.

Ed, witness. The song and the Book of the Law are both called witnesses against Israel. A witness in Israel's courts was someone who had seen and could testify; here a text serves that role, standing as a record of what Israel was told.

Yetser, inclination or intention, literally something formed. God says he knows Israel's inclination even before bringing them into the land (verse 21). The same word describes humanity's inclination toward evil in Genesis 6:5 and 8:21, and later Jewish thought developed it into the idea of the evil inclination within every person.

christ: The promise at the heart of this chapter, “He will never leave you nor forsake you” (verse 6), is quoted in Hebrews 13:5 and applied to every believer: God's presence with his people did not end with Joshua. The transfer of leadership from Moses, who could not enter the land, to Joshua, who led the people in, has also long been seen by Christian readers as a pattern. Joshua's name is the Hebrew form of the name Jesus, and Hebrews 4:8 draws a contrast between the partial rest Joshua gave and the fuller rest that remains for God's people. The chapter's honest prediction that God's people would fail also frames the New Testament's hope: faithfulness would finally require a mediator and a new covenant, with the law written on the heart rather than only placed beside the ark. These connections are drawn by later Scripture, not stated in this chapter.

hard.q: If God knew Israel would turn away, why did he go ahead with the covenant?
hard.a: The chapter does not hide the tension: God predicts apostasy while still bringing Israel into the land and binding them to himself. Readers have answered in different ways. Some emphasize that foreknowledge does not cause the failure; Israel remains fully responsible, and the song is given precisely so they cannot claim ignorance. Others stress that God's covenant rests on his oath to the patriarchs rather than on Israel's performance, so his commitment is not cancelled by their failure; Deuteronomy 30 has already promised restoration beyond judgment. Theological traditions that emphasize divine sovereignty and those that emphasize human freedom both find support here, and both agree on the chapter's pastoral point: God's persistence with a people he knows will fail is itself an act of grace.

questions: Moses tells both Israel and Joshua to be strong and courageous because God goes with them. Where do you need courage that rests on God's presence rather than on your own ability?
The law was to be read to everyone, including children and foreigners. What does this suggest about who Scripture is for and how it should be shared?
God tells Moses to teach a song so the people would remember. What songs or habits have shaped what you remember about God?
